An independent transcription pass over the same two pages, which never saw this file, derived the same five letters (CCCCD) from the page images alone; that pass is the genuine independent check.
why: Read the exponents straight off the formula: one power of length, one of mass and minus two of time, that is mass times length divided by time squared. Newton's second law makes force the product of mass and acceleration, and acceleration is length per time squared, so force has exactly those dimensions. Velocity is length per unit time, \([L^{1}M^{0}T^{-1}]\), and carries no mass term at all. Acceleration is \([L^{1}M^{0}T^{-2}]\), which differs from the given formula only by the missing mass. Work is force times displacement and so carries a second power of length, \([L^{2}M^{1}T^{-2}]\).

_method: SECOND DERIVATION, not a blind pass — see the note on Ex Q.1 (i).
why: The area of a rectangle is the product of its two sides, and for a product the percentage errors add. Each side is measured with a 1% error, so the area carries \(1\% + 1\% = 2\%\). Quoting 1% would treat the area as though it depended on a single measurement rather than two. Halving the figure to one half of a percent inverts the rule that applies here: a percentage error is halved when a square root is taken, not when two quantities are multiplied. Since the correct figure of 2% does appear among the alternatives, the catch-all 'none of the above' is not needed.

_method: SECOND DERIVATION, not a blind pass — see the note on Ex Q.1 (i).
why: A light year is defined as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in one year, about \(9.46 \times 10^{15}\) m. The word 'year' in its name refers to the time over which the light travels, not to the quantity the unit measures, and that is the trap this question sets. This chapter lists the light year alongside the astronomical unit and the parsec as the units astronomers use for large distances. Time is measured in seconds, mass in kilograms and luminous intensity in candela, so a unit of length cannot serve for any of those.

_method: SECOND DERIVATION, not a blind pass — see the note on Ex Q.1 (i).
why: Kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), so its dimensions are mass times the square of a velocity: \([M^{1}] \times [L^{1}T^{-1}]^{2} = [L^{2}M^{1}T^{-2}]\). Work is force times displacement, \([L^{1}M^{1}T^{-2}] \times [L^{1}] = [L^{2}M^{1}T^{-2}]\), which is the same — as it has to be, since the work-energy theorem equates work done with the change in kinetic energy. Force on its own is \([L^{1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\), short by one power of length. Acceleration is \([L^{1}M^{0}T^{-2}]\) and carries no mass. Pressure is force per unit area, \([L^{-1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\), where the power of length is negative.

_method: SECOND DERIVATION, not a blind pass — see the note on Ex Q.1 (i).
why: The trap here is that a unit can belong to a fundamental quantity without being the SI base unit for it. The centimetre measures length and the kilogram measures mass, both fundamental quantities; the centigrade degree measures temperature, which is fundamental too, even though its SI base unit is the kelvin. The volt is different in kind, because it measures potential difference, which is defined as work done per unit charge and so is assembled out of other units: \(1\ \mathrm{V} = 1\ \mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{C}^{-1}\), with dimensions \([L^{2}M^{1}T^{-3}I^{-1}]\). A unit built up from the base units in that way is called a derived unit.
